summary: Describes a mechanism that emulates full two-way connectivity between nodes that are connected by a one-way link, such as satellite receive-only links. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If a radio can only listen, not talk, this sets up a secret return path so it can still behave like a two-way connection.

questions: how to use one way satellite links with ip
how do satellite receive-only links work with ip
subtitle: How receive-only links, such as satellite downlinks, can behave like normal two-way links by sending their return traffic through tunnels over the Internet.

tldr.problem: Internet routing and upper-layer protocols assume links are bidirectional, but a receive-only interface such as a satellite receiver simply discards anything the network layer tries to send out of it.
tldr.mechanism: A receiver wraps outgoing link-layer packets in a tunnel (GRE is recommended) and sends them over the Internet to a feed, which unwraps them and puts them onto the one-way link. Feeds announce their tunnel end-points to receivers with a small protocol called DTCP.
tldr.outcome: The network layer sees an ordinary bidirectional broadcast link, so ARP, IP and routing protocols work unchanged. Address resolution over long delays and tunnel authentication are left unsolved or unspecified.

today: RFC 3077 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The One-Way Link Problem
sections.content:
Internet routing and upper-layer protocols assume that directly connected hosts can talk to each other over the same link. A unidirectional link (UDL), for example a broadcast satellite link, breaks that assumption.

The text calls receive-only interfaces "dumb" and send-only interfaces "deaf". A datagram handed to the driver of a receive-only interface is simply discarded. So if Recv 1 runs ping against a feed on the same network, the packet never leaves, and routing protocols between directly connected routers stop behaving properly.

This RFC describes a link-layer tunneling mechanism that hides the one-way nature of the link from the network layer and above. It is not designed for a pair of nodes joined by two unidirectional links in opposite directions.
sections.eli5: Imagine a walkie-talkie that can only listen. Anyone who asks it a question gets no answer, because it cannot talk back. This RFC gives it a hidden way to answer.

sections.title: Feeds, Receivers and the Topology
sections.content:
A receiver has receive-only connectivity to the UDL. A feed is a router that sends on the UDL: a send-only feed can only send, while a receive capable feed can also receive. A feed MUST be a router.

Every node also has at least one ordinary bidirectional interface connected to the Internet. Tunnels run between these bidirectional interfaces, so they must be reachable over an IP infrastructure. The mechanism supports any number of receivers and one or more feeds, though the number of feeds is expected to be small.

Addresses on the unidirectional interfaces come from the same IP network. Addresses on the bidirectional interfaces generally come from different networks, with the Internet routing between them.
sections.eli5: The feed is like a big loudspeaker that everyone can hear. Each listener also has a normal phone line to call the loudspeaker operator, who then says the message out loud for them.

sections.title: Emulating a Broadcast Network
sections.content:
The RFC chooses to emulate a broadcast-capable link-layer network. Working at the link layer lets existing protocols run unchanged and allows ARP, and other network-layer protocols besides IP, to work immediately.

It lists six scenarios that would work on a real broadcast link: a receiver sending to a feed, to everyone, or to another receiver; and a feed sending to a send-only feed, to everyone, or to a receiver or receive capable feed. Scenario 6 already works over the one-way link, so the tunnel has to supply scenarios 1 to 5.

Regular IP forwarding over the emulated network also works, because the next hop at a receiver is the unidirectional-link address of another router.
sections.eli5: The goal is to make the one-way link look exactly like a normal shared network, so no program has to know anything unusual is going on.

sections.title: How Receivers and Feeds Tunnel Packets
sections.content:
On a receiver, a datagram sent out of the unidirectional interface gets its MAC header, then is wrapped in an IP header addressed to a feed's bidirectional interface (the tunnel end-point). If the destination MAC is a feed, the packet goes to that feed. If it is a broadcast or multicast address, or belongs to another receiver, it goes to the default feed.

A feed decapsulates what it receives, and the original MAC header is intact. What happens next depends on the destination MAC address:

  • Its own address: delivered locally, as if it had come from the unidirectional link.
  • Another receiver: sent over the unidirectional link, and not delivered locally.
  • Broadcast or multicast from a receiver: sent to all send-only feeds, over the unidirectional link, and delivered locally.

To reach a send-only feed, a feed also tunnels packets to it, using a manually configured list of the other feeds. A receiver that sent a broadcast to the default feed will hear its own packet come back over the link, so correct filtering as in RFC 1112 must be applied.
sections.eli5: A listener sends their message through the phone line to the loudspeaker operator. The operator reads it out so the right person, or everyone, hears it on the loudspeaker.

sections.title: Dynamic Tunnel Configuration Protocol
sections.content:
Feeds are configured by hand, but receivers cannot be. The Dynamic Tunnel Configuration Protocol (DTCP) lets receivers discover feeds and keep a list of working tunnel end-points. Feeds periodically send HELLO messages over the unidirectional link, so DTCP only ever flows from feeds to receivers. It runs over UDP.

A HELLO carries a version, a command (JOIN for "I am up", LEAVE for "I am shutting down"), an interval, a sequence number, a flag for send-only or receive-capable, the IP version, a tunnel type and a list of the feed's bidirectional addresses in preferred order.

A receiver adds an entry for a new feed on JOIN, resets its timer when the sequence number is unchanged, and deletes the entry on LEAVE. If no JOIN arrives before the timer expires, the entry is removed, whether the feed went down or the whole link did. That stops receivers from tunneling into a dead end-point.

The default feed is chosen independently by each receiver as a matter of local policy. The RFC gives the lowest round trip time as an example.
sections.eli5: The loudspeaker operators keep shouting "I am here, call me on this number!" Listeners write down the numbers, and cross one off if the shouting stops.

sections.title: The HELLO Message and Constants
sections.content:
The HELLO message starts with two 4-bit fields, Vers and Com, then an 8-bit Interval and a 16-bit Sequence. The next word holds 3 reserved bits, the 1-bit F flag (0 for send-only, 1 for receive-capable), a 4-bit IP Vers (4 or 6), an 8-bit Tunnel Type and an 8-bit Nb of FBIP, followed by that many feed addresses of 32 or 128 bits each.

Tunnel Type is an IP protocol number, and 47 (GRE) is recommended. Receivers MUST use the tunnel form the feed names.

Constants: DTCP_VERSION is 1, HELLO_INTERVAL is 5 seconds, the announcement group is 224.0.0.36, and HELLO_PORT is 652. HELLO_LEAVE is 3 times the advertised interval, 15 seconds by default. Packets are sent with a TTL of 1.
sections.eli5: The "I am here" shout has a fixed form: who is shouting, whether they are staying or leaving, how often they will shout, and a list of phone numbers to call.

sections.title: Tunnel Encapsulation with GRE
sections.content:
The mechanism assumes the link hardware supports unicast and broadcast MAC addressing, so receivers can filter incoming packets without caring what they carry. Because whole link-layer packets are encapsulated, a feed can filter after decapsulation as if the data had come straight from the link.

The RFC recommends Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE, RFC 2784), which can carry arbitrary packets and use IP as the delivery protocol. A tunneled packet is an IP delivery header addressed to the feed's tunnel end-point with protocol 47, then a GRE header whose type is the MAC type of the UDL, then the MAC packet as payload.

The feed's administrator decides what encapsulation receivers must use and sets the tunnel type in the HELLO. Values other than 47 are possible, but their interpretation must be agreed between feeds and receivers and is not defined here.
sections.eli5: The message is put into an envelope addressed to the operator. Inside is the original message, still with its own address label, untouched.

sections.title: Open Issues and Security
sections.content:
The RFC admits two problems it does not solve. First, reactive address resolution such as ARP may work poorly on a link with long delays. A GEO satellite link has a delay of about 250 milliseconds, so a feed that is forwarding at high data rates may run out of buffer space while waiting for an ARP reply. An ad-hoc fix is to derive the MAC address from the IP address by a simple transformation, where the receiver card allows it.

Second, tunnels open the door to unauthorised access, including ARP and IP spoofing. The RFC says this can be countered by authenticating all tunnels, for example with AH (RFC 2402), but specifies no mechanism. Routing protocols running over the mechanism MUST use authentication when available. The link contents are easy to receive, so link-layer security is suggested for sensitive data, and the feed addresses in HELLO messages may also be sensitive.
sections.eli5: Anyone nearby can overhear the loudspeaker, and anyone could try to pretend to be a listener. So the RFC suggests checking who is really calling in.

fields.name: Vers
fields.desc: DTCP version number; MUST be DTCP_VERSION.

fields.name: Interval
fields.desc: Seconds between HELLO messages; must be greater than 0.

fields.name: Sequence
fields.desc: Random at boot, incremented when HELLO contents change.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: 0 is send-only feed, 1 is receive-capable feed.

fields.name: IP Vers
fields.desc: 4 or 6, the IP version of the feed addresses.

fields.name: Tunnel Type
fields.desc: IP protocol number of the tunnel; 47 (GRE) is recommended.

fields.name: Nb of FBIP
fields.desc: Number of feed bidirectional addresses that follow.

layers.label: IP delivery header
layers.detail: Destination is the feed tunnel end-point (FBIP); IP protocol is GRE (47)

layers.label: GRE header
layers.detail: Type is the MAC type of the unidirectional link
